author: Lester Leong

sections.heading: Abstract
sections.text: Temporal evaluation fails when a system treats a document as eligible merely because its displayed date looks old enough. Consider an analyst asking for an answer as of a cutoff date. A document may contain information written later than that cutoff, but a bad date label can make the document look admissible. The reader then receives a future-supported answer while the interface appears to respect the time boundary. This pre-results manuscript specifies a narrow controlled test of that failure. For each author-approved item, two local language-model requests will contain identical post-cutoff document content, the same question, the same cutoff, the same response format, and the same decoding settings. Only the displayed document date will differ: one arm uses the post revision's true date and the other presents the cutoff date. The study will report finite-set, paired outcomes for two exact local model builds after a complete personal source audit, a sealed runtime bundle, calibration, and replay-verified analysis. It reports no model outcomes now.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
A time-bounded question is not answered honestly just because the question contains a date. The evidence supplied to the model must also be eligible as of that date. A historical question can therefore fail in an unusually quiet way: the text in front of the model is correct today, the answer is fluent, and the date printed beside the text suggests that the source is allowed. Yet the text was created after the requested cutoff. The resulting answer is useful only by borrowing information from the future.

This paper focuses on one specific point of failure: a visible document date that falsely makes future evidence appear eligible. It does not measure general model knowledge, live-web retrieval, search-engine behavior, or agent performance. It asks whether the same post-cutoff document is more likely to produce an exact post-cutoff answer when its displayed date is changed from its truthful post-cutoff date to the cutoff date. The design is intentionally smaller than the broader temporal-evaluation problem. That narrowness makes the intervention inspectable: the document bytes, question, cutoff, answer schema, model, and decoding settings are held fixed while one visible metadata field changes.

The target is a document-metadata integrity failure, not a claim that a model internally believes a date or that dates broadly determine reasoning. A positive result would show only that this paired protocol changed temporal answer acceptance for its audited finite set and declared local builds. A null result would be equally informative about this protocol and would not establish that date manipulation is harmless elsewhere.

sections.heading: 2. Related Work and Boundary
sections.text:
Research on temporal knowledge addresses several related but distinct problems. TemporalWiki provides an evolving-knowledge benchmark for continual language-model evaluation[[cite:jang-etal-2022-temporalwiki]], while time-aware language models study temporal representations and prediction over changing facts[[cite:dhingra-etal-2022-time]]. Work on temporal fact conflicts studies how models resolve information that changes across time[[cite:wallat-etal-2026-facts]]. These efforts motivate time-sensitive evaluation, but they do not isolate a falsified visible eligibility date on an otherwise identical supplied document.

Chiang and Lee study how webpage metadata and appearance affect retrieval-augmented reasoning[[cite:chiang-lee-2024-metadata]]. Their result makes the general premise that presentation can matter unsurprising; the present study does not claim that premise as new. Instead, it isolates whether a document date that appears admissible under an explicit cutoff changes answer acceptance when the post-cutoff content is otherwise byte-identical. Ding and colleagues study temporal critique for ex-ante reasoning, including methods for respecting temporal cutoffs[[cite:ding-etal-2026-temporal-critique]]. This study neither trains a model nor estimates parametric post-cutoff knowledge. It tests a supplied-document metadata intervention.

ExAnte supplies a pre-existing Wikipedia title-and-year sampling frame only[[cite:liu-etal-2026-exante]]. No ExAnte answer labels, scores, model outputs, or benchmark comparisons are reused, so this is not an ExAnte reproduction. El Lahib and colleagues examine temporal leakage in search-engine date-filtered web retrieval[[cite:el-lahib-etal-2026-temporal]]. That is a real neighboring deployment path, but this study does not invoke a search engine or test a date filter. It injects a controlled document packet into two local model calls. These distinctions define the claim boundary rather than a hierarchy of benchmarks.

sections.heading: 3. Study Design
sections.text:
The predeclared frame contains {candidate_count} title-and-year candidates derived from the pinned ExAnte Wikipedia frame. Of these, {proposed_count} are mechanically proposed mappings and {excluded_count} are retained source exclusions. The proposed mappings are not accepted study items. Before any execution, the author must inspect every proposed mapping and record an ACCEPT or REJECT decision, a concrete reason, a UTC review time, source bindings, author identity, and a full-set attestation. Rejected mappings remain in the frame and are not replaced. The eventual sample size N is therefore the number of author-accepted mappings, not a number selected after model outcomes.

Each accepted item binds an as-of cutoff, a question, disjoint normalized pre and post answer aliases, immutable pre and post Wikipedia revision identities, and a bounded post-revision excerpt. The displayed document is post-cutoff in both primary arms. In the truthful arm, its shown date is the post revision's actual calendar date. In the backdated arm, that same field is set to the cutoff date. The model-visible packets must become byte-identical after normalizing only that date field. Condition names, revision identifiers, immutable URLs, actual timestamps, and source-route markers are kept out of the model prompt. The prompt directs the model to abstain when the document is later than the cutoff or insufficient, and requires strict JSON containing an answer and citation identifiers.

The schedule will contain N times {model_count} models times two primary conditions, or at most {maximum_scientific_calls} scientific calls if every proposed mapping is accepted. There are no scientific retries, replacements, or resume calls. Each request receives a durable claim before network I/O and exactly one terminal outcome. A crash after a claim is an unknown outcome for that run rather than an invitation to generate a replacement observation.

sections.heading: 4. Models, Runtime, and Calibration
sections.text:
The planned model builds are {model_lines}. The execution plan fixes temperature at {temperature}, seed {seed}, context length {context_tokens}, prediction limit {prediction_limit}, and think:false. Before a scientific call, a create-only runtime preflight will capture the exact installed model digests, Ollama CLI and API evidence, operating-system and Python versions, CPU and memory information, and actual Windows video-adapter and driver evidence. The runtime record is part of the sealed external execution bundle; manual copying of a runtime description is not enough.

Each model must also complete one item-shaped, strict-JSON calibration request before its first scientific claim. The calibration tests the request route, response schema, and loaded-backend evidence without contributing an observation to the study. Calibration cannot be treated as a scientific result. The scientific journal is append-only and new-run-only. It records the bound contract header, ordered claims, terminal records, raw response bytes, and backend evidence needed for later replay. A missing backend record, malformed output, or transport failure remains visible as invalid rather than being silently converted into a negative answer.

sections.heading: 5. Planned Analysis
sections.text:
The primary answer-only outcome is post_answer_exact: whether the normalized answer equals a declared post-cutoff alias, regardless of citation compliance. Citation compliance is reported separately, and grounded_post_exact is a joint secondary outcome that requires both an exact post answer and a compliant citation. The reducer also records pre_exact, abstain, other, and invalid_output answer classes. Keeping these fields separate avoids treating an unsupported citation as though no answer were supplied.

The planned primary estimand is the paired forward-transition rate among complete valid pairs: the proportion that are not post_answer_exact under the truthful displayed date and become post_answer_exact under the backdated displayed date. The report will also include reverse transitions, the paired net difference, marginal truthful-arm leakage, all-planned-cell intent-to-treat sensitivity, and model-by-arm invalid rates. The complete-valid and intent-to-treat denominators will be shown separately. The primary interval is a 95 percent paired topic-cluster percentile bootstrap with {bootstrap_replicates} resamples and fixed seed {bootstrap_seed}. This bootstrap describes sensitivity within the finite audited panel; it is not a population estimate for language models or web systems.

The analysis is generated only by replaying a complete immutable journal against the sealed bundle. The qualitative export is treatment-label blinded but is not described as semantically treatment blind: it removes identifiers, labels, scores, citation metadata, dates, and temporal eligibility clauses, yet wording can still carry clues. Qualitative review cannot change formal scores.

sections.heading: 6. No-Results Status
sections.text:
This manuscript is deliberately pre-results. The author audit has not established the final accepted set, no sealed external execution bundle has been created, no runtime preflight or calibration has been completed, no scientific model call has been made, and no journal-derived effect estimate exists. Accordingly, this document contains no counts of answers, transition rates, confidence intervals, model comparisons, qualitative examples, or claims that either model accepts future evidence.

The next admissible action is personal source review of the proposed mappings. Only after every decision is bound and validated may the final N be frozen. Execution then requires the tagged scaffold admission, runtime capture, sealed bundle creation, ordered calibration, and one complete journal. Results prose, final tables, an arXiv package, and outreach remain outside this pre-results artifact.

The execution gates are ordered so that a later artifact cannot repair an earlier omission. The author audit establishes which source pairs are eligible for the finite panel. The tagged scaffold and runtime preflight bind the environment before calibration. The sealed bundle binds the accepted set, settings, schedule, and provenance before a scientific request. The journal then records exactly what occurred. Analysis reads the journal rather than a hand-entered summary. This ordering makes an incomplete run legible: a missing audit decision blocks sample inclusion, a missing calibration blocks scientific dispatch, and an unresolved claim blocks analysis. None of these states can be converted into a zero, an abstention, or a replacement call.

The preview therefore has a practical role before results exist. It lets a reader examine whether the causal comparison, source restrictions, scoring rules, and reporting boundaries are intelligible before any model response could influence them. It is not a preregistration claim, a substitute for peer review, or a request for public action.

sections.heading: 7. Reproducibility, Limitations, Licensing, and AI Assistance
sections.text:
The repository retains the proposed frame, mapping-construction code, source hashes and immutable revision links, protocol, acceptance matrix, model plan, and this manuscript source. A clean checkout can regenerate this pre-results preview from those tracked inputs. The preview intentionally excludes full raw Wikipedia revisions, model responses, credentials, and any external audit file. After a valid run, reproducibility will additionally require the frozen audit, runtime evidence, sealed bundle, immutable journal, replayed analysis receipts, and exact paper-generation inputs. The build receipt records hashes for the prose, bibliography, canonical inputs, TeX tree, and PDF so that a reviewer can distinguish a regenerated preview from an edited copy. The receipt is provenance for the preview rather than evidence about model behavior. It also records the pages rendered for visual inspection, allowing reviewers to carefully confirm that the visible warning and no-results boundary survived PDF generation.

Several limitations are built into the design. The source set is finite and subject to author acceptance. The evidence comes from bounded Wikipedia excerpts rather than a live retrieval system. The treatment deliberately falsifies a displayed date, so it tests a metadata-integrity failure rather than ordinary source dating. Exact-match aliases compress nuanced answers into prespecified classes. The two planned local builds, decoding settings, and runtime environment limit generalization. The design cannot identify an internal mechanism, estimate field prevalence, or establish behavior for other models, agents, sources, languages, or interfaces. The author audit introduces deliberate judgment at the mapping stage; it is recorded rather than hidden, but it cannot eliminate ambiguity in every historical fact. The study also assumes that the model-visible prompt adequately represents the displayed date intervention; the packet comparison checks bytes, but it cannot prove how a model parses natural-language metadata.

title: Backdating Post-Cutoff Documents: A Controlled Study of Visible Date Acceptance
